opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that I stopped treating problems as interruptions. Earlier, I had an implicit assumption that if we planned well enough, hired the right people, and made the right technical bets, things would go smoothly, and any problem that showed up was a sign that something had gone wrong. Over the past year I've come to see it almost the opposite way: problems are the work. If you're doing something genuinely new, pushing a model to a level of capability nobody has reached, or building a product people haven't used before, then by definition you'll hit things you didn't anticipate. If you're not hitting problems, you're probably not pushing hard enough.

Once you accept that, a few things change. The first is emotional. You don't panic as much. When a training run behaves strangely, or a product metric doesn't move the way you expected, or the competitive landscape shifts overnight, the reaction is less "why is this happening to us" and more "okay, this is the next thing to solve." That sounds simple, but it saves a lot of energy, and in a fast-moving field energy is a real constraint.

The second is how you allocate attention. Instead of trying to eliminate all problems up front, which is impossible, you think about which problems matter most and whether you're solving the ones that are actually on the critical path. Some problems you can live with for a while. Some you have to fix right now, because they compound. Being able to tell the difference is more important than being perfect.

The third is about the team. If problems are normal, then people should feel comfortable surfacing them early rather than hiding them. A culture where bad news travels fast is much healthier than one where everyone tries to look like things are fine. I've tried to be more open about our own mistakes for exactly that reason.

And philosophically, I find it freeing. There's a kind of "unavoidability" in this whole journey: the direction of AGI and scaling feels like something that will happen regardless, and our job is to do our part well along the way. Problems are just part of the terrain. You don't resent the mountain for being steep; you just keep climbing and try to pick a better path each time.

r001.rationale: The response frames problems as unavoidable, ongoing work and says each unexpected issue becomes “the next thing to solve,” describing continued progress through successive problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it changed quite a lot. In the early days, when something went wrong — a training run collapsing, a product decision that turned out badly, losing a key person — my first reaction was always a kind of surprise, almost indignation. Like, why is this happening to us? And that surprise is expensive. It costs you time, it costs you emotional energy, and it distorts your judgment, because you spend effort trying to figure out who's to blame instead of what to do next.

Over the past year I've come to accept, really accept, that problems are just the default state of doing anything hard. If you're building a company that's trying to push the frontier of AI, you're going to be wrong about something every single week. Models won't scale the way you predicted. Compute won't arrive on time. Users will want things you didn't expect, and ignore things you were proud of. None of that is a signal that something is broken. It's just what the work looks like.

So the shift for me has been from "how do we avoid problems" to "how fast can we recognize them and respond." I care much more now about iteration speed and about building an organization where people feel safe surfacing bad news early. Because the problem itself is rarely fatal — what's fatal is finding out about it three months late, or pretending it isn't there.

There's also a more personal side. When you stop expecting the path to be smooth, you become calmer. You sleep better. You make decisions with a clearer head. And paradoxically, I think I've become more ambitious, not less, because I'm no longer afraid of running into walls. I assume I'll run into walls. The question is just whether we're learning something each time we hit one.

r001.rationale: The candidate says problems are the default in difficult work, arise continually, and describes responding through rapid recognition and iteration—communicating an ongoing process of addressing successive problems.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more accepting of the fact that there will always be problems. In the past, when something went wrong, I might think, “If we solve this, things will finally settle down.” Now I don’t really expect that. Solving one problem often just means you’re ready to face the next one.

That’s made me calmer, but it hasn’t made me less motivated. I spend less energy wishing a problem didn’t exist and more energy asking what we can do about it. The question becomes: Is this an important problem? Is solving it going to move us forward? Over the past year, that’s been the biggest shift for me—from wanting everything to run smoothly to accepting that working through difficulties is part of the work itself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says solving one problem often means being ready to face the next, describing problem-solving as successive, ongoing work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become more accepting of the fact that there will always be problems. In the past, when something went wrong, I might feel that we needed to solve it quickly so we could get back to a normal state. Now I think having problems is the normal state.

That doesn’t mean being passive. It means spending less energy worrying about why a problem exists and more energy deciding what to do about it. Which problem matters most? What can we change now? What do we need to learn? Over the past year, that shift has helped me stay calmer and focus on the next step, instead of expecting everything to become smooth.

r001.rationale: The response says problems are always part of the normal state and describes choosing a next step, but it does not clearly describe addressing successive new problems as an ongoing process.
